original.target_description: Study 1: independent-samples t-test comparing estimated age of the ambiguous woman between the youngest and oldest observer groups (18–22 versus 49–68 years).

n.sample_role: Participants in the two analytic extreme-age groups
n.exclusions: Restricted to USA respondents; required both attention checks, valid demographics, and an estimated age older than 18. Final eligible sample 393; extreme-group comparison further restricted by observer age.
n.location: p. 4, Results, paragraph beginning “To obtain a stronger result” (publisher full-text HTML)
n.quote: very-youngest 10% of participants (aged between 18 and 22 years, n = 40) and the very-oldest 10% of participants (aged between 49 and 68 years, n = 45)

es.location: p. 4, Results, paragraph beginning “To obtain a stronger result” (publisher full-text HTML)

p.location: p. 4, Results, paragraph beginning “To obtain a stronger result” (publisher full-text HTML)

replication.target_description: Study 1: one-tailed independent-samples t-test of estimated ambiguous-figure age, youngest versus oldest 8.94% (22 participants per group); intentionally differs from original 10% to avoid splitting tied ages.

n.sample_role: Participants in the analytic extreme-age comparison (22 per age group)
n.exclusions: 14 of 260 recruited participants excluded following eligibility checks (person and female identification), leaving 246. Extreme-group comparison additionally restricted to youngest/oldest 8.94%.
n.location: p. 4, Results, Primary analyses: replication of original findings, paragraph beginning “In the original paper” (publisher full-text HTML)
n.quote: This resulted in a sample of n = 44 with 22 participants in each age group.

es.location: p. 4, Results, Primary analyses: replication of original findings, paragraph beginning “In the original paper” (publisher full-text HTML)

p.location: p. 4, Results, Primary analyses: replication of original findings, paragraph beginning “In the original paper” (publisher full-text HTML)

reported_success.quote: In this study, we replicated the finding that older participants estimate the woman in the figure to be significantly older than young participants do.

notes: Youngest/oldest contrast matched independently. Replication explicitly selects 8.94% rather than 10% to avoid arbitrarily excluding tied ages. Original p retained exactly as printed. Success refers to age-estimate finding; replication authors reject the original perceptual/social-group explanation.
